title: The Mountain Walk
theme: Again and again in Scripture God meets his people on a mountain: Abraham offers his son, Israel receives the Law, Solomon builds the Temple, Jesus is lifted up, and the risen Lord ascends. Walking these heights in order shows one hill-country story in which a sacrifice, a covenant and a house of God are drawn together in the end in Christ.

stops.quote: Now take your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.
stops.what: God tests Abraham and tells him to take Isaac, his beloved only son, to a mountain in the land of Moriah to offer him there.
stops.echo: Isaac carries the wood and is spared, and the Church reads this as a sign of the Father giving his only Son. Later tradition places the Temple on this same mountain (2 Chronicles 3:1).

stops.quote: All of Mount Sinai smoked, because the LORD descended on it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace, and the whole mountain quaked greatly.
stops.what: On the third day there is thunder, lightning, a thick cloud and a trumpet blast, and the LORD comes down on the mountain while the people tremble below.
stops.echo: On this mountain God makes a covenant and gives the Law and the pattern of the tent of meeting. The Church reads the Law as the first stage of a covenant that Christ will bring to completion on another mountain.

stops.quote: Then Solomon began to build the LORD’s house at Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where the LORD appeared to David his father
stops.what: Solomon begins to build the Temple in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, on the threshing floor David had prepared.
stops.echo: The Chronicler names the Temple hill with the same name as Abraham’s mountain, so that the offering of Isaac and the worship of the Temple stand on one ridge. The prophets then look to this mountain as the place where all nations will gather.

stops.quote: the mountain of the LORD’s house shall be established on the top of the mountains
stops.what: Isaiah sees that in the latter days the mountain of the LORD’s house will be set above all other mountains and will draw many peoples.
stops.echo: The Church reads this vision as fulfilled when the Gospel goes out from Jerusalem to all nations. It also finds in it the Church, the new house of God for every people.

stops.quote: He went out, bearing his cross, to the place called “The Place of a Skull”, which is called in Hebrew, “Golgotha”, where they crucified him
stops.what: Jesus carries his own cross out of the city to Golgotha, where he is crucified between two others.
stops.echo: The Church sees in Jesus the beloved Son who carries the wood and whom the Father does not spare, as Isaac was spared. The sacrifice of the old mountains is gathered here into one offering.

stops.quote: he was taken up, and a cloud received him out of their sight.
stops.what: From the Mount of Olives Jesus is taken up into the sky while the disciples look on, and two men in white tell them he will return in the same way.
stops.echo: The Church reads the Ascension as Christ entering heaven, the true holy place, and sending his disciples to carry the Gospel from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. The mountain walk ends where the hope of his return begins.

title: Water and Baptism
theme: Israel is saved by passing through water: the Red Sea, the Jordan, and the cleansing of Naaman. The Church reads these as pointing ahead to Baptism, where Jesus himself goes down into the Jordan and the Spirit comes upon him.

stops.quote: The children of Israel went into the middle of the sea on the dry ground; and the waters were a wall to them on their right hand and on their left.
stops.what: Moses stretches out his hand, the LORD drives the sea back with a strong east wind all night, and Israel walks through on dry ground.
stops.echo: The New Testament reads the Red Sea as a type of Baptism, 1 Corinthians 10:1-2. The Church sees Israel set free from slavery through water as a sign of the baptized being set free from sin.

stops.quote: The priests who bore the ark of the LORD’s covenant stood firm on dry ground in the middle of the Jordan; and all Israel crossed over on dry ground, until all the nation had passed completely over the Jordan.
stops.what: When the priests carrying the ark step into the river, the waters stop flowing, and all Israel crosses on dry ground near Jericho.
stops.echo: Where the Red Sea ends slavery, the Jordan crossing opens the way into the promised land. The Church reads Baptism as both: leaving the old life and entering the inheritance that God promised.

stops.quote: Elijah took his mantle, and rolled it up, and struck the waters; and they were divided here and there, so that they both went over on dry ground.
stops.what: Elijah rolls up his mantle and strikes the Jordan, and the waters divide so that he and Elisha cross over on dry ground.
stops.echo: Elisha receives the prophetic spirit just after crossing, and the Church sees in this a pattern: the crossing of water and the gift of the Spirit belong together, as they do in Baptism.

stops.quote: Then went he down and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God; and his flesh was restored like the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.
stops.what: Naaman, the Syrian commander, obeys the prophet’s word and dips himself seven times in the Jordan, and his leprosy is healed.
stops.echo: The Church reads Naaman’s healing as a sign of the cleansing of Baptism, where the flesh is made new like a little child’s. Like him, the baptized are washed by obeying a plain word of God.

stops.quote: “Go, wash in the pool of Siloam”(which means “Sent”). So he went away, washed, and came back seeing.
stops.what: Jesus tells a man born blind to wash in the pool of Siloam, and he returns able to see.
stops.echo: The Church has long read this washing as a picture of Baptism as illumination, in which the baptized are given sight. The pool whose name means Sent also points to Jesus, who is himself the one sent.

stops.quote: Jesus, when he was baptized, went up directly from the water: and behold, the heavens were opened to him. He saw the Spirit of God descending as a dove, and coming on him.
stops.what: Jesus comes from Galilee to the Jordan and is baptized by John, and the Spirit descends on him while the Father’s voice declares him his beloved Son.
stops.echo: The Church sees Jesus entering the waters of the Jordan to sanctify water for Baptism. In Baptism the baptized are joined to the Son and the Spirit and the Father’s voice is spoken over them as adopted children.

stops.quote: John also was baptizing in Enon near Salim, because there was much water there.
stops.what: John continues to baptize at Enon near Salim, where there was plenty of water, and people come to him and are baptized.
stops.echo: John’s baptism prepares the way, and the Church sees the full gift of the Spirit coming at Pentecost, when Peter tells the crowd to be baptized for the forgiveness of sins (Acts 2:38).

title: The Garden Walk
theme: Scripture begins in a garden and ends in a city with the tree of life, and the Gospel story passes through gardens along the way. Following the places that echo Eden shows how Christ’s agony and burial reopen what was lost.

stops.quote: The fourth river is the Euphrates. The LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.
stops.what: Genesis names the rivers that flow from Eden, including the Euphrates, and tells that God put the man in the garden to cultivate and keep it. Eden itself is not on the map, so the Euphrates stands as the nearest named landmark.
stops.echo: Man is placed in a garden to serve God, and loses it by disobedience. The prophets then promise that God will make the wilderness like Eden again.

stops.quote: For the LORD has comforted Zion.
stops.what: Isaiah proclaims that the LORD has comforted Zion and will make her wasteland like Eden and her desert like the garden of the LORD.
stops.echo: The promise of a restored Eden is attached to the holy city. The Church reads it as fulfilled in Christ, who gathers a new people in a place of life and joy.

stops.quote: he went out with his disciples over the brook Kidron, where there was a garden, into which he and his disciples entered.
stops.what: After the Last Supper, Jesus crosses the Kidron brook with his disciples and enters a garden.
stops.echo: John pointedly sets the Passion in a garden, and the Church reads the new Adam freely entering a garden to undo the first Adam’s disobedience.

stops.quote: He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.”
stops.what: Jesus comes to a place called Gethsemane, becomes sorrowful and troubled, and prays on his face to the Father.
stops.echo: In Eden man said no to the Father’s will, and in Gethsemane the Son says yes. The Church sees in this prayer the heart of the Passion, where obedience heals the first disobedience.

stops.quote: Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden. In the garden was a new tomb in which no man had ever yet been laid.
stops.what: In the place where Jesus was crucified there is a garden with a new tomb, and Jesus is laid there.
stops.echo: Death and burial happen in a garden, so that new life can begin in a garden too. The Church reads the tomb as the place where the new creation starts on the third day.

stops.quote: Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Who are you looking for?” Jesus said to her, “Mary.”
stops.what: At the tomb in the garden, Mary Magdalene meets the risen Jesus, and she knows him only when he speaks her name.
stops.echo: In John’s account Mary takes him for the gardener, and the Church sees in this a sign that the new Adam is again tending the garden. The story ends in the city of Revelation, where the tree of life stands again.

stops.quote: He showed me a river of water of life, clear as crystal, proceeding out of the throne of God and of the Lamb
stops.what: John sees a river of the water of life flowing from the throne of God, with the tree of life on either bank, bearing fruit every month and healing the nations.
stops.echo: The garden that was lost in Genesis is restored in the city of God. The Church reads this as the final fulfilment of the promise to all who are in Christ.

title: Bread and Manna
theme: God feeds his people with bread in the wilderness, again at the hands of his prophets, and finally in the person of Jesus. The Church sees these loaves and meals leading step by step to the Eucharist.

stops.quote: Moses said to them, “It is the bread which the LORD has given you to eat.
stops.what: In the wilderness of Sin the people find a small round thing on the ground like frost, and Moses tells them it is bread from the LORD.
stops.echo: Manna is bread from heaven for a hungry people. Jesus takes it up in John 6, and the Church reads manna as a sign of the Eucharist.

stops.quote: The jar of meal didn’t run out and the jar of oil didn’t fail, according to the LORD’s word, which he spoke by Elijah.
stops.what: At Zarephath a widow obeys Elijah, and her jar of meal and jar of oil do not run out for many days.
stops.echo: God’s word again provides bread where there is none. The Church sees in this a sign of the Lord who will feed the hungry crowds with a few loaves.

stops.quote: He arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb, God’s Mountain.
stops.what: An angel wakes the exhausted Elijah and gives him a cake baked on the coals and a jar of water, and he walks forty days to Horeb in the strength of that food.
stops.echo: Elijah is carried by heavenly food to the mountain of God, as Israel was in the wilderness. The Church reads this as a sign of the Eucharist as food for the journey.

stops.quote: But he said to them, “You give them something to eat.”
stops.what: When a crowd follows Jesus to a deserted place, he welcomes them and teaches them, and when evening comes he tells the Twelve to feed them.
stops.echo: In Luke the feeding that follows is told with the actions of the Eucharist: he takes, blesses, breaks and gives (Luke 9:16). The Church sees the miracle pointing ahead to the altar.

stops.quote: This is the bread which came down out of heaven—not as our fathers ate the manna and died. He who eats this bread will live forever.
stops.what: In the synagogue at Capernaum Jesus contrasts the manna eaten by the ancestors with the bread that has come down from heaven, which gives life forever.
stops.echo: Jesus himself names manna and says that he is the true bread. The Church reads this as the promise of the Eucharist, which the Last Supper then fulfils.

stops.quote: He took bread, and when he had given thanks, he broke and gave it to them, saying, “This is my body which is given for you. Do this in memory of me.”
stops.what: At the Last Supper in Jerusalem Jesus takes bread, gives thanks, breaks it and gives it to the apostles, saying that it is his body given for them.
stops.echo: The promise of John 6 is fulfilled: the bread is his body. The Church celebrates this each time the Mass is offered in obedience to his command.

stops.quote: When he had sat down at the table with them, he took the bread and gave thanks. Breaking it, he gave it to them.
stops.what: On the evening of Easter, the risen Jesus sits at table with two disciples at Emmaus, and they recognize him as he breaks the bread.
stops.echo: The Church sees in this the pattern of the Mass, where the Lord is known in the breaking of the bread after the Scriptures have been opened. The walk ends at a table that is still set today.

title: The City of David
theme: The story of David’s house runs from a shepherd boy in Bethlehem to a king in Jerusalem, and then to a child born in David’s city. The Church reads this line of kings as leading to Christ, whose kingdom is the heavenly Jerusalem.

stops.quote: Then Samuel took the horn of oil and anointed him in the middle of his brothers. Then the LORD’s Spirit came mightily on David from that day forward.
stops.what: Samuel anoints the youngest son of Jesse in the middle of his brothers, and the Spirit of the LORD comes on David.
stops.echo: The anointed one, which is what the word Messiah means, begins in small Bethlehem. The Church sees in David a first image of the king to come.

stops.quote: Nevertheless David took the stronghold of Zion. This is David’s city.
stops.what: David captures the Jebusite stronghold of Zion in Jerusalem, and it becomes known as David’s city.
stops.echo: Zion becomes the royal and holy hill. In the Church’s reading, the name Zion later stands for the people of God and for the heavenly city.

stops.quote: I will set up your offspring after you, who will proceed out of your body, and I will establish his kingdom. He will build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom forever.
stops.what: God promises David, through the prophet Nathan, that a descendant of his will be given a kingdom and a throne that last forever.
stops.echo: Solomon builds the Temple, yet the promise reaches further. The Church reads the throne that lasts forever as fulfilled in Jesus, son of David.

stops.quote: But you, Bethlehem Ephrathah,
stops.what: Micah addresses Bethlehem Ephrathah, the small clan town, and promises a ruler who will stand and shepherd in the strength of the LORD.
stops.echo: The prophecy points back to David’s own town. The Church sees in it the birthplace of Christ, the shepherd king.

stops.quote: Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judea, to David’s city, which is called Bethlehem, because he was of the house and family of David
stops.what: Joseph goes up to Bethlehem because he is of David’s house, and there Mary gives birth to her firstborn son and lays him in a feeding trough.
stops.echo: The promise to David comes to rest in a stable. Luke wants us to see the child as the son of David, born in David’s city.

stops.quote: Blessed is the King who comes in the name of the Lord! Peace in heaven, and glory in the highest!
stops.what: As Jesus nears Jerusalem at the descent of the Mount of Olives, his disciples praise God and call him the King who comes in the Lord’s name.
stops.echo: David’s heir enters David’s city, and the crowd greets him as king. The Church sees this as the coming of the true Son of David, though his kingdom is not of this world.

stops.quote: But you have come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem
stops.what: The letter to the Hebrews tells the believers that they have already come to Mount Zion and to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem.
stops.echo: The earthly Zion points to the Church and to the final city. Revelation 21:2 describes it as the holy city coming down out of heaven from God.

title: Exile and Return
theme: Jerusalem falls and Israel is taken to Babylon, yet God does not abandon his people: he speaks to them in exile and brings them home to rebuild. The Church reads this movement from loss to restoration as a pattern fulfilled in Christ, who proclaims freedom to captives.

stops.quote: He burned the LORD’s house, the king’s house, and all the houses of Jerusalem.
stops.what: Nebuzaradan, captain of the Babylonian guard, enters Jerusalem and burns the Temple, the palace and every great house.
stops.echo: The Temple, the sign of God’s presence, is destroyed and the people are driven away. The prophets teach that this is judgment but not the end.

stops.quote: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down.
stops.what: The exiles sit by the rivers of Babylon and weep, and their captors ask them for songs.
stops.echo: The psalm gives Israel a voice of grief that the Church still prays. It remembers Zion even in a strange land.

stops.quote: as I was among the captives by the river Chebar, the heavens were opened, and I saw visions of God.
stops.what: Ezekiel, among the captives by the river Chebar, sees the heavens opened and visions of God.
stops.echo: God is not bound to the Temple and is present with the exiles. The Church sees here a sign that God’s presence goes with his people wherever they are.

stops.quote: I, Daniel, understood by the books the number of the years about which the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah the prophet, for the accomplishing of the desolations of Jerusalem, even seventy years.
stops.what: In Babylon Daniel reads in the books of Jeremiah that the desolation of Jerusalem is to last seventy years.
stops.echo: Daniel responds to the promise with prayer. The Church honours this pattern: God’s promise is met by the repentance and prayer of his people.

stops.quote: They sang to one another in praising and giving thanks to the LORD, “For he is good, for his loving kindness endures forever toward Israel.”
stops.what: When the returned exiles lay the foundation of the new Temple, the priests and Levites praise the LORD with trumpets and cymbals, and the people shout.
stops.echo: The return fulfils the promise given in exile. Yet the new Temple is only a beginning, and the Church sees the true return in the gathering of God’s people in Christ.

stops.quote: The Spirit of the Lord is on me,…to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord.…Today, this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.
stops.what: In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus reads from Isaiah about the Lord’s Spirit and the acceptable year, and says that this Scripture is fulfilled today.
stops.echo: Isaiah’s words of freedom for captives were spoken to a people recovering from exile. The Church reads Jesus as bringing the true return, release from sin and death.

stops.quote: She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, greets you. So does Mark, my son.
stops.what: Peter sends greetings from Babylon, together with Mark, to Christians scattered in Asia Minor.
stops.echo: The Church reads Babylon here as Rome, a traditional reading rather than the text’s own claim. The Church lives as a people in exile, longing for the city to come.

title: The Shepherd
theme: God is the shepherd of Israel, and he raises up shepherd kings from David to the one who calls himself the good shepherd. This walk follows the places where a shepherd is named, from the boy anointed in Bethlehem to Peter being told to feed Christ’s sheep.

stops.quote: Samuel said to Jesse, “Are all your children here?”
stops.what: Samuel asks Jesse whether all his sons are present, and the youngest, tending sheep, is brought in and anointed.
stops.echo: God chooses the boy from the sheepfold to rule his people. The shepherd’s care is the pattern for the king’s care.

stops.quote: The LORD said to you, ‘You will be shepherd of my people Israel, and you will be prince over Israel.’
stops.what: The tribes of Israel come to David at Hebron, recall the LORD’s word that he would shepherd Israel, and anoint him king.
stops.echo: Kingship is named as shepherding. The Church sees David as a figure of Christ, the shepherd of God’s people.

stops.quote: He shall stand, and shall shepherd in the strength of the LORD,
stops.what: Micah promises that a ruler will come from Bethlehem Ephrathah and shepherd the people in the strength of the LORD.
stops.echo: The promised shepherd comes from the same small town as David. The Church sees this fulfilled in Jesus.

stops.quote: There were shepherds in the same country staying in the field, and keeping watch by night over their flock.
stops.what: Shepherds in the fields keep watch by night, and an angel tells them a Savior has been born in David’s city.
stops.echo: The first to hear the news of the birth are shepherds. The Church sees the good news going first to the humble and the watchful.

stops.quote: The next day, he saw Jesus coming to him, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!
stops.what: At Bethany beyond the Jordan, John the Baptist sees Jesus and calls him the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.
stops.echo: The shepherd is also the lamb. The Church reads this as a sign that he will give his own life for the flock.

stops.quote: I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.
stops.what: Jesus says he is the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep, unlike a hired hand who flees when the wolf comes.
stops.echo: This is the fulfilment of God’s promise to shepherd his people himself. The Church sees the Cross as the shepherd’s act of laying down his life.

stops.quote: So when they had eaten their breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you love me more than these?”
stops.what: After breakfast on the shore, the risen Jesus asks Simon Peter three times whether he loves him.
stops.echo: In John 21:15-17 Jesus entrusts his sheep to Peter, and the Church reads in this the shepherding office handed on to Peter and his successors.

title: Peter’s Road
theme: Peter’s road runs from his home on the Sea of Galilee to Rome, following the places where Jesus calls him, names him, forgives him and sends him. The Church reads the same road as the foundation of her own life.

stops.quote: He rose up from the synagogue and entered into Simon’s house.
stops.what: At Capernaum Jesus leaves the synagogue, enters Simon’s house and heals his mother-in-law of a fever.
stops.echo: Jesus makes Simon’s house a base for his ministry. The Church sees Peter’s home as where he first draws close to the Lord.

stops.quote: But Simon Peter, when he saw it, fell down at Jesus’ knees, saying, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.”
stops.what: After a huge catch at Jesus’ word, Simon Peter falls at Jesus’ knees and says he is a sinful man.
stops.echo: Jesus tells him he will catch men (Luke 5:10). The Church sees that Peter is called as a sinner, not as someone who has earned it.

stops.quote: Simon Peter answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”
stops.what: Near Caesarea Philippi Jesus asks his disciples who they say he is, and Peter answers that he is the Christ, the Son of the living God.
stops.echo: Jesus answers by naming Peter the rock on which he will build his Church and giving him the keys of the Kingdom. The Church reads this as the basis of Peter’s special place among the apostles.

stops.quote: He said to him the third time, “Simon, son of Jonah, do you have affection for me?”
stops.what: After the Resurrection, Jesus asks Peter three times whether he loves him, once for each of his three denials.
stops.echo: Jesus restores Peter and gives him the flock to feed (John 21:17). The Church reads this as the commission to shepherd all the sheep.

stops.quote: Peter said to them, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.
stops.what: On Pentecost, Peter tells the crowd to repent and be baptized, and about three thousand are added that day.
stops.echo: The one who denied the Lord now preaches him. The Church sees the beginning of her mission, led by Peter, in this first sermon.

stops.quote: Peter opened his mouth and said, “Truly I perceive that God doesn’t show favoritism; but in every nation he who fears him and works righteousness is acceptable to him.
stops.what: In the house of the centurion Cornelius, Peter says that God shows no favoritism and accepts those in every nation who fear him.
stops.echo: Peter opens the door of the Church to the Gentiles. The Church reads the keys given to him as used here to let the nations in.

stops.quote: But when Peter came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he stood condemned.
stops.what: Paul tells how Peter came to Antioch and drew back from eating with Gentiles, and Paul opposed him openly.
stops.echo: Even Peter is corrected over the truth of the Gospel, and the Church honours the honesty of Scripture. At Antioch the disciples were first called Christians (Acts 11:26).

stops.quote: She who is in Babylon, chosen together with you, greets you. So does Mark, my son.
stops.what: Peter sends greetings from Babylon, together with Mark, to the churches he is writing to.
stops.echo: The Church reads Babylon here as Rome, where tradition holds that Peter taught and died. The Bishop of Rome is therefore called Peter’s successor.
